verse.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy our brother,
to the holy ones in Colossae, the faithful brothers and sisters in Christ: grace to you and peace from God our Father.
verse.note: The traditional 'saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. The Greek word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'. The Greek here could also be read as two adjectives, 'to the holy and faithful brothers and sisters'.

verse.text: We always give thanks to God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you,
for we have heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love you have for all the holy ones
because of the hope stored up for you in the heavens. You heard of this hope before, in the word of truth, the good news
verse.note: The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase that most English translations flatten to 'heaven'. The plural is kept wherever the Greek has it and God's dwelling is meant.

The Greek word meant an announcement of good news, such as a victory or a ruler's accession. 'Gospel' is the traditional rendering and remains common, but today it suggests a book or a religious term more than a piece of news. Several modern translations also use 'good news'.

verse.text: that has come to you. Just as it is bearing fruit and growing in all the world, so it has been among you too, from the day you heard it and came to know the grace of God in truth.
You learned it from Epaphras, our beloved fellow slave, who is a faithful servant of Christ on our behalf,
verse.note: The word is built on the ordinary Greek term for a slave, someone owned by a master, here Christ. Most translations soften it to 'fellow servant'. 'Slave' is used here so that it stays distinct from the different word translated 'servant' later in the same verse.

Early manuscripts are divided between 'on our behalf' and 'on your behalf'; the two differ by one letter in Greek. The SBLGNT reads 'our', which would mean Epaphras worked in Colossae as Paul's representative. Many translations follow the other reading.

verse.text: and who has also told us of your love in the Spirit.
For this reason we too, from the day we heard, have not stopped praying for you and asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding,
so that you may walk in a way worthy of the Lord and please him in everything: bearing fruit in every good work and growing in the knowledge of God,
empowered with all power according to the might of his glory for all endurance and patience, with joy
giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you for a share in the inheritance of the holy ones in the light.
He rescued us from the authority of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love,
in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation,
verse.note: In Jewish usage 'firstborn' often meant rank and inheritance rights, not order of birth; in the Greek Psalms it is used of the Davidic king as supreme over other kings. Most interpreters therefore take the phrase to mean supremacy over creation, and some translations say 'firstborn over all creation'. The grammar alone could also mean the first of created things, a reading argued since antiquity, though the next verse sets him apart from 'all things' that were created.

verse.text: for in him all things were created, in the heavens and on the earth, the visible and the invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. All things have been created through him and for him.
And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together.
And he is the head of the body, the assembly. He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that in everything he himself might come to hold first place,
verse.note: A first-century hearer knew this word as a civic gathering of citizens and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is always visible.

verse.text: for in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell

note.term: all the fullness was pleased to dwell
note.traditional: it pleased the Father that in him should all fullness dwell

verse.note: The Greek does not name who 'was pleased'. It can be read with 'all the fullness' as subject, as here, or with God understood: 'God was pleased to have all his fullness dwell in him'. On either reading the fullness is God's own, as 2:9 makes explicit. In verse 20, 'to him' could refer to Christ, matching 'for him' in verse 16, or to God ('to himself'), as many translations take it.

verse.text: and through him to reconcile all things to him, making peace through the blood of his cross, [through him], whether things on the earth or things in the heavens.
verse.note: The brackets reproduce those of the SBLGNT. This repeated 'through him' is present in some important early manuscripts and absent from others, and the editors regard its originality as doubtful. It could have been dropped by copyists as redundant or added by accidental repetition.

verse.text: And you, who were once alienated and hostile in mind, in your evil deeds—
but now you have been reconciled in his body of flesh through death—so as to present you holy, unblemished and beyond reproach before him,
verse.note: Most manuscripts and most translations read 'he has now reconciled', which gives a smooth sentence. The SBLGNT follows a small number of early witnesses that read the passive 'you have been reconciled', judging that copyists smoothed the harder wording. On this reading the sentence breaks off and resumes, and the translation keeps that broken structure with dashes.

verse.text: if indeed you continue in the faith, founded and steadfast, not shifting from the hope of the good news that you heard, which has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven, and of which I, Paul, became a servant.
Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ for the sake of his body, which is the assembly.

note.term: what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ
note.traditional: that which is behind of the afflictions of Christ

verse.note: The meaning is disputed. The letter has just said that Christ's death fully reconciles, so few interpreters think Paul means that death was insufficient. The common views are that the sufferings are those Christ's people must still endure in union with him, or the quota of distress that Jewish expectation placed before the end, of which Paul takes a share on the assembly's behalf.

verse.text: I became its servant according to the stewardship from God that was given to me for you, to make the word of God fully known,
the mystery that was hidden for ages and generations but has now been revealed to his holy ones.
verse.note: In the Greek of this period, and especially in the Greek version of Daniel, this word means a secret that God holds and discloses. It does not mean a puzzle or something that cannot be understood. Here it is God's long-concealed plan, now made public.

verse.text: To them God chose to make known what is the wealth of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.
verse.note: The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations'; in the plural, in Jewish usage, it means the non-Jewish peoples. This translation uses 'Gentiles' for that sense and 'nations' where peoples as such are meant. Both renderings translate the same Greek word.

The Greek 'you' is plural, and the preposition can mean 'in' or 'among'. The phrase may therefore mean Christ dwelling within believers, or Christ present among you Gentiles, which would echo 'among the Gentiles' just before. The traditional 'in you' is kept, and the two senses do not exclude each other.

verse.text: Him we proclaim, warning every person and teaching every person in all wisdom, so that we may present every person mature in Christ.
To this end I labor, struggling in keeping with his working, which works in me with power.
For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those in Laodicea, and for all who have not seen my face in the flesh,
that their hearts may be encouraged, as they are knit together in love and come into all the wealth of the full assurance that understanding brings, into the knowledge of God’s mystery, Christ,

note.traditional: the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ

verse.note: The manuscripts give this phrase in many different forms, including the longer one behind the King James Version. Most textual critics judge the short and abrupt 'of the mystery of God, Christ' to be original, with the other forms as scribal attempts to smooth it. 'Christ' is most naturally read as explaining what the mystery is, as translated; 'the mystery of the God of Christ' is grammatically possible but unlikely.

verse.text: in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.
I say this so that no one may deceive you with plausible-sounding arguments.
For even if I am absent in the flesh, I am still with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.
So then, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him,
rooted and being built up in him and made firm in the faith, just as you were taught, overflowing with thanksgiving.
See to it that no one carries you off as plunder through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ.
verse.note: In the first century 'philosophy' covered any organized body of teaching with its way of life, religious as well as intellectual, and Jewish writers used the word of Judaism and its schools. A single Greek article joins 'philosophy' and 'empty deceit', so one thing is in view. It is a particular teaching on offer at Colossae, not the discipline of philosophy as such.

note.traditional: rudiments of the world (KJV); elemental spirits (RSV, NRSV, ESV); elementary principles (NASB)

verse.note: The Greek word means the basic components of something: letters of the alphabet, first principles of a subject, or the physical elements. In writers of the period the full phrase 'elements of the world' regularly means the physical elements (earth, water, air, fire) of which the world was thought to be made, and that plain rendering is kept here. Many scholars instead understand spiritual powers believed to govern the cosmos, a sense not clearly attested for the word until later, and others understand 'elementary teachings'. The question is unresolved; the phrase recurs in verse 20.

verse.text: For in him all the fullness of deity dwells bodily,
and you have been made full in him, who is the head of every ruler and authority.
In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, in the stripping off of the body of flesh, in the circumcision of Christ,
verse.note: This can mean a circumcision that Christ performs or that belongs to him, in contrast to the physical rite. It can also be a metaphor for Christ's own death, in which his 'body of flesh' was stripped away. On the first reading 'the body of flesh' is the believer's old self; on the second it is Christ's physical body. The translation leaves both open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.
verse.note: The Greek pronoun can also be read 'in whom', continuing the series of 'in him' phrases that runs through verses 6 to 11. Most translations take it of baptism, as here, since baptism is the nearest noun and burial and rising form a natural pair.

verse.text: And when you were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made you alive together with him. He forgave us all our trespasses,
erasing the record of debt that stood against us with its decrees and was hostile to us; he has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross.
verse.note: The Greek word means a handwritten document, and in everyday use a note of debt written in the debtor's own hand. Ink of the period could be washed or wiped off, which is the picture behind 'erasing'. How the 'decrees' relate to the document, whether as its terms or as the grounds of the debt, is debated.

verse.text: He stripped the rulers and the authorities and made a public show of them, leading them in triumphal procession in him.
verse.note: The verb is the counterpart of the noun 'stripping off' in verse 11 and literally refers to taking off clothing. Most modern translations read 'disarmed', with God stripping the powers of their weapons or dignity. Many early Greek interpreters instead took it as 'stripped off from himself', with Christ shedding the powers at the cross. 'Stripped' keeps the echo of verse 11 and suits the picture of captives displayed in a triumph.

note.term: leading them in triumphal procession in him

verse.note: The verb refers to the Roman triumph, in which a victorious general paraded defeated enemies through the city as a public humiliation. 'The rulers and the authorities' here are spiritual powers, not human officials. The final phrase can equally be translated 'in it', meaning the cross; 'in him' assumes that God is still the subject, as in verse 13, and that the triumph takes place in Christ.

verse.text: So do not let anyone judge you over what you eat or drink, or in the matter of a festival, a new moon, or a sabbath.
These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.
verse.note: The Greek word is 'body', used here in a common contrast between a shadow and the solid thing that casts it. Because 'body' also means the church in this letter (verse 19), some hear a second sense: the reality is found in the body of Christ. Most translations render 'substance' or 'reality', as here.

verse.text: Let no one who delights in self-abasement and the worship of angels disqualify you, going on in detail about what he has seen, puffed up without cause by his fleshly mind,
verse.note: This is the ordinary word for humility, which is elsewhere a virtue. Here and in verse 23 it names something the rival teachers insist on and take pride in, apparently a practice: in Jewish and early Christian usage 'humbling oneself' often referred to fasting and similar rigors. 'Self-abasement' marks that sense; several modern versions use it or 'asceticism', while others keep 'humility' or 'false humility'.

This is usually understood as worship offered to angels. The Greek can equally mean the worship that angels themselves offer, in which case the teachers claimed to witness or join the heavenly worship in visions, an idea found in Jewish texts of the period. Scholarship is divided.

note.term: going on in detail about what he has seen
note.traditional: intruding into those things which he hath not seen

verse.note: This is one of the most obscure phrases in the letter. The verb basically means to enter or set foot on, and can mean to go into a subject in detail. It also appears in later inscriptions for entering a sanctuary after initiation, so 'which he saw on entering', of a visionary experience, is also possible. Later manuscripts add 'not' ('what he has not seen'), which lies behind the King James rendering; the earliest witnesses lack it.

verse.text: and not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with the growth that comes from God.
If you died with Christ to the elements of the world, why, as though still living in the world, do you submit to decrees:

text.q: “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch,”

verse.text: which all concern things destined to perish with use, according to human commands and teachings?
Such things do have a reputation for wisdom, with their self-chosen worship and self-abasement and severity to the body, but they are of no value against the gratification of the flesh.

note.term: of no value against the gratification of the flesh
note.traditional: not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh

verse.note: The Greek of this verse is compressed and its syntax is disputed. The rendering here, that such rules have no value in restraining self-indulgence, is the majority view. The words can also be taken to mean that the rules are of no value and serve only to gratify the flesh, that is, the pride of the one who keeps them.

verse.text: So if you were raised with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
Set your minds on the things above, not on the things on the earth,
for you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
When Christ, your life, is revealed, then you too will be revealed with him in glory.
verse.note: Most English versions have 'when Christ appears'. The Greek verb means to make visible what was concealed, and it answers 'hidden' in the previous verse: the life now hidden with Christ will be brought into the open when he is. 'Revealed' keeps that connection, and some modern translations render it the same way.

verse.text: Put to death, then, the parts of you that are on the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed, which is idolatry.

note.term: the parts of you that are on the earth
note.traditional: your members which are upon the earth

verse.note: The Greek says literally 'the limbs that are on the earth' and then lists vices, as though they were body parts to be killed. The phrase 'on the earth' deliberately repeats verse 2. Many modern versions paraphrase as 'whatever in you is earthly'; the stranger wording here is the Greek's own.

verse.text: Because of these the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience.
verse.note: Some important early manuscripts lack these words, and many scholars think they were added by copyists from the parallel at Ephesians 5:6. The SBLGNT prints them as original. 'Sons of' is a Semitic idiom for people characterised by something; here, the disobedient.

verse.text: Among them you too once walked, when you were living in these things.
verse.note: The Greek pronoun can be masculine ('among whom', the sons of disobedience) or neuter ('in which', the vices just listed). The first is chosen here because it avoids making the second half of the verse a repetition of the first. If the last phrase of verse 6 is not original, only 'in which' is possible.

verse.text: But now you too must lay them all aside: wrath, rage, malice, slander, foul talk from your mouth.
Do not lie to one another, since you have stripped off the old self with its practices

note.traditional: seeing that ye have put off

verse.note: The Greek participles in verses 9 and 10 can give the reason for the command ('since you have stripped off... and have put on') or be commands themselves ('strip off... and put on'). Most interpreters take them as the reason, pointing back to a change that has already happened. The image is of taking off and putting on clothing.

The Greek is literally 'the old human being', traditionally 'the old man'. 'Self' is the usual modern rendering and is used here for clarity. The expression is wider than an individual's personality, though: verse 11 describes the new one as a sphere where ethnic and social divisions no longer hold, and many scholars see a contrast between the old humanity and the new one created in Christ.

verse.text: and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of the one who created it,
where there is no Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free, but Christ is all and in all.
verse.note: 'Barbarian' was the Greek term for anyone who did not speak Greek and so stood outside Greek culture. Scythians, peoples from north of the Black Sea, were proverbial in the Greek world as the wildest of barbarians. The pair moves from the outsider to the most extreme outsider.

verse.text: So, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, put on heartfelt compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience,
verse.note: 'Meekness' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a person who is not harsh or self-assertive. 'Gentleness' or 'humility' is the usual rendering in modern translations.

verse.text: bearing with one another and forgiving each other if anyone has a complaint against someone. Just as the Lord forgave you, so you also must forgive.
And over all these put on love, which is the bond of completeness.
verse.note: The phrase is compressed and can be taken more than one way: love is the bond that produces completeness or maturity, or love is the perfect bond that holds the other virtues, or the community, together. The rendering keeps the Greek's own brevity. 'Over all these' continues the clothing image of verse 12, but could also mean 'above all'.

verse.text: And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, the peace to which you were called in one body. And be thankful.
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, as you teach and admonish one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with gratitude in your hearts to God.
verse.note: The Greek word can mean 'grace' or 'gratitude'; the surrounding calls to thankfulness in verses 15 and 17 favour the second. The punctuation of the verse is also uncertain. 'In all wisdom' may go with 'dwell' or with 'teach and admonish', and 'with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs' may go with the teaching or with the singing. 'In you' can also be read 'among you'.

verse.text: And whatever you do, in word or in deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
Husbands, love your wives and do not grow bitter toward them.
Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing in the Lord.
Fathers, do not provoke your children, so that they do not lose heart.
Slaves, obey your human masters in everything, not with work done only to be seen, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord.
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'masters according to the flesh'. 'Master' here and 'Lord' are the same Greek word throughout verses 22 to 24. The instruction turns on that: slaves have masters on the human level, but their real master is the Lord Christ.

verse.text: Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, as for the Lord and not for people,
knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. It is the Lord Christ you serve as slaves.
verse.note: Under Roman law a slave could not normally inherit; inheritance belonged to sons. The promise of an inheritance from the Lord gives slaves the standing of heirs.

note.term: It is the Lord Christ you serve as slaves.
note.traditional: for ye serve the Lord Christ

verse.note: The verb comes from the same root as 'slaves' in verse 22, which the rendering brings out. Its form can be a statement ('you are serving') or a command ('serve the Lord Christ'). Most translations take it as a statement, as here, though some scholars prefer the command.

verse.text: For the one who does wrong will be paid back for the wrong he did, and there is no favoritism.
Masters, give your slaves what is just and fair, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven.
verse.note: The Greek word for a slave's 'master' is the same word translated 'Lord' when used of Christ in the preceding verses. Paul's point depends on that identity: slave owners are themselves under a kyrios. English has to choose between 'master' and 'lord', so the wordplay is only partly visible.

note.traditional: that which is just and equal

verse.note: The second noun can mean 'equality' as well as 'fairness' or 'equity'. Most interpreters take it here as even-handed, equitable treatment rather than a call to treat slaves as social equals, and the translation follows that view. The stronger sense cannot be ruled out.

verse.text: Persevere in prayer, keeping alert in it with thanksgiving,
praying at the same time for us too, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am in chains,
so that I may make it plain, as I ought to speak.
Conduct yourselves with wisdom toward outsiders, making the most of the opportunity.

note.term: making the most of the opportunity

verse.note: The verb is a marketplace word, 'to buy up', and the noun means a particular or opportune time, not time in general. The older rendering 'redeeming the time' suggests rescuing time from something. Most modern translations take the phrase, as here, to mean seizing the present opportunity.

verse.text: Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you know how you ought to answer each person.
Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant and fellow slave in the Lord, will tell you all my news.
verse.note: The word is built on the ordinary Greek term for a slave, the same one used of household slaves in verse 1 and of Epaphras in verse 12. 'Servant' is kept in this translation for a different Greek word, which also appears in this verse. Many translations soften both to 'servant'. Paul's language describes belonging to a master, not employment.

verse.text: I am sending him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how things are with us and that he may encourage your hearts,
together with Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you everything that is happening here.
Aristarchus, my fellow captive, greets you, as does Mark, the cousin of Barnabas (you have received instructions about him; if he comes to you, welcome him),
verse.note: This is not Paul's usual word for a prisoner. It means someone taken captive in war. Most translations have 'fellow prisoner'. Whether Aristarchus was literally confined with Paul or the term is a military metaphor for shared hardship in Christ's service is uncertain.

verse.text: and Jesus who is called Justus. Of those from the circumcision, these alone are fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.
verse.note: This is a standard way of saying 'Jews', here Jewish believers. Paul is saying that Aristarchus, Mark and Jesus Justus are the only Jewish Christians working alongside him at this time. It follows that Epaphras, Luke and Demas, named next, were Gentiles.

verse.text: Epaphras, who is one of you, a slave of Christ, greets you. He is always struggling for you in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God.
verse.note: The verb can mean 'fully convinced, assured' or 'filled, brought to completion'. Older translations have 'complete in all the will of God'; many modern ones have 'fully assured'. Either fits a letter much concerned with fullness and with firmness of conviction.

verse.text: For I can testify of him that he labors hard for you and for those in Laodicea and those in Hierapolis.
Luke, the beloved physician, greets you, and so does Demas.
Greet the brothers and sisters in Laodicea, and Nympha and the assembly in her house.
verse.note: The Greek word meant a gathering of people. It was used for a city's citizen assembly and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel assembled. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and is well understood, but it now suggests a building or institution. Here the group is one that meets in a private home.

note.term: Nympha and the assembly in her house
note.traditional: Nymphas, and the church which is in his house

verse.note: The manuscripts differ: some read 'her house' (a woman, Nympha), some 'his house' (a man, Nymphas), and some 'their house'. The name in the Greek text is identical for either gender apart from its accent, which the earliest manuscripts did not write. Most modern editions and translations judge 'her' to be original, with the change to 'his' made by later copyists.

verse.text: And when this letter has been read among you, see that it is also read in the assembly of the Laodiceans, and that you also read the one from Laodicea.
verse.note: Paul refers to a letter that the Colossians are to obtain from the neighbouring assembly at Laodicea. It is usually thought to be a letter of Paul to the Laodiceans that has not survived. Some scholars identify it with the letter known as Ephesians. A later Latin 'Epistle to the Laodiceans' is not genuine.

verse.text: And tell Archippus, “See that you fulfill the service you received in the Lord.”
verse.note: The noun belongs to the same word-family as 'servant' in verse 7 and means a task carried out for another. 'Ministry' is the traditional rendering, but it now suggests a clerical office. What Archippus's assignment was is not known.

verse.text: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.

note.traditional: by the hand of me Paul

verse.note: Letters were normally dictated to a scribe. At this point Paul takes the pen and adds a closing line himself, as a sign that the letter is authentic, much as a signature would be. He does the same at the end of several other letters.
